titleStmt.title: Breaking down scats: degradation of DNA from greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) faecal pellets

analytic.title: Breaking down scats: degradation of DNA from greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) faecal pellets

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Isolating DNA from scats (faeces) of threatened species is a valuable, non-invasive method for identifying individuals. To establish whether genotyping of greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) individuals from faecal pellets collected in the field can be useful for population monitoring, an understanding of the DNA degradation rates is necessary. To determine the relationship between time and degradation of bilby faecal DNA, and assess whether a two-step elution process during extraction results in better-quality DNA, faecal pellets were collected from captive individuals, maintained under seminatural conditions, then harvested at known periods. DNA was amplified from faecal pellets with a 99% success rate and error rates of less than 5% up to 14 days after deposition. The amplification rate decreases, and the rate of allelic dropout increases with time, but DNA can still be amplified at rates above 60% and error rates below 15% at 90-180 days. We found that a second elution step was unnecessary, with more DNA amplified over a longer period using the first eluate. Viable DNA exists on bilby faecal pellets for a long period after deposition, which is useful for obtaining genetic samples for population monitoring programs and studies on population genetics.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Utilising scats (faecal pellets) as opposed to sourcing tissue or blood for DNA samples has the benefit of reducing direct impacts to species being studied (Murphy et al. 2000;Piggott and Taylor 2003b;Vynne et al. 2012;Ramón-Laca et al. 2015). This is particularly useful in the case of threatened or rare species, of which many may be vulnerable to disturbance (e.g. Puechmaille and Petit 2007;Baldwin et al. 2010). Isolation of DNA from faeces has been successfully undertaken for several threatened species across a variety of environments, from snow leopards (Panthera uncia) in the alpine regions of Nepal (Karmacharya et al. 2011), to mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei) in the forests of Uganda (Nsubuga et al. 2004), and African elephants (Loxodonta africana africana) in savannah grasslands (Archie et al. 2003). Although it is now a well established method for identifying individuals (Ernest et al. 2000;Adams and Waits 2006;Brinkman et al. 2010a;Rodgers and Jane cka 2013), few studies have incorporated faecal DNA as a component of ongoing monitoring programs compared with direct sampling techniques, mainly due to the limitations associated with obtaining DNA from non-invasive samples (Waits and Paetkau 2005;Schwartz et al. 2007). More recently researchers have developed an increased awareness of the need to understand and evaluate the specific degradation rates of the faecal DNA of the target species to ensure the quality of genotyping approaches (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b;Panasci et al. 2011;DeMay et al. 2013;Woodruff et al. 2015).

Time has been found to have a significant effect on the amplification rates of faecal DNA. Murphy et al. (2007) analysed the effects of time on the degradation of DNA from brown bear (Ursus arctos) faeces and found that genotyping errors increased over time across different environmental conditions. Sample age, particularly 1-3 days since deposition, reduced the ability to amplify DNA. Santini et al. (2007) also found faecal DNA from wolves (Canis lupus) to degrade quickly with a significant difference in the rate of amplification after just three days. Panasci et al. (2011) found an increase in amplification failure and errors with time and recommended that coyote faeces of less than five days since deposition are preferable for DNA extraction. However, they were also able to successfully amplify DNA from some samples after this time. Woodruff et al. (2015) studied faecal DNA degradation from the Sonoran pronghorn (Antilocapra americana sonoriensis) and also found genotyping reliability to decrease over time, with the most significant drop in amplification (decrease of 61%) occurring between 7 and 14 days since deposition. Piggott (2004) studied the impacts of time on faecal DNA of European red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) and brushtailed rock wallabies (Petrogale penicillata) in Australia. For both species, she found that age since deposition resulted in a decline in amplification rates and an increase in genotyping error rates. No amplification was obtained from samples 180 days since deposition and the highest-quality DNA and reliable genotyping was obtained from samples up to seven days from deposition.

DNA has been successfully extracted from faecal pellets of many threatened marsupial species in Australia (e.g. Alacs et al. 2003;Piggott et al. 2006;Walker et al. 2009;Ruibal et al. 2009;Smith et al. 2009;Wedrowicz et al. 2013). One of these species, the greater bilby (Macrotis lagotis) is a burrowing marsupial that was once widespread across most of mainland Australia (Marlow 1958;Southgate 1990;Friend 1990;Gordon et al. 1990;Johnson and Southgate 1990;Abbott 2001Abbott , 2008;;Bradley et al. 2015) but now is found in only 20% of its former range (Southgate 1990). A better understanding of bilby density, abundance and population distribution is critical in determining appropriate strategies for the conservation and management of this species, with this being noted as a key research priority and knowledge gap for the bilby particularly in Western Australia (Bradley et al. 2015;Cramer et al. 2016).

The bilby is a cryptic, trap-shy and wide-ranging species (McGregor and Moseby 2014), which makes the implementation of traditional and direct fauna monitoring techniques, including capture-mark-recapture methods through trapping, very difficult for this species due to the intensity, time and high level of resources that would be required (Southgate et al. 1995;Lollback et al. 2015). Non-invasive methods to monitor fauna species that use evidence of the target species, such as tracks, burrows, dens, pellets and scats, are becoming increasingly preferred methods, particularly for species that are highly dispersed or elusive (Piggott and Taylor 2003a), including the bilby (Southgate et al. 2005;Southgate and Moseby 2008;Burrows et al. 2012;Lollback et al. 2015). Bilby faecal pellets are easily identified in the field as they have a distinct physical appearance and can often be observed amongst other bilby signs, particularly at diggings (Southgate et al. 2005). They are also easy to collect and store, involving reduced resources and effort than would otherwise be required for trapping, and can provide an alternative source of information for monitoring (Southgate 2005;Lollback et al. 2015).

Previous success of DNA extraction from greater bilby faecal pellets provides a reliable and efficient non-invasive method for identifying bilby individuals (Smith et al. 2009), and may therefore be useful in gaining an understanding of population size and density.

The degradation of DNA from bilby faecal pellets, however, has not yet been explored. The need to understand faecal DNA degradation rates when using this as a source for identifying individuals in a species monitoring program was raised by Piggott (2004), particularly with species such as the bilby, where populations are often remote and individuals are at low densities, making it difficult to source fresh samples regularly.

Studies on faecal samples from both herbivorous and carnivorous species have shown that the age of the faecal sample contributes significantly to the ability to extract and amplify DNA, with fresh samples resulting in more reliable amplification with fewer genotyping errors than found with older samples (Lucchini et al. 2002;Piggott 2004;Santini et al. 2007;Panasci et al. 2011). Therefore, it is useful to know, particularly for monitoring or for obtaining DNA for other genetic studies, up to what age samples still yield DNA and what the quality of DNA is at a particular age.

DNA extracted from faecal matter includes DNA from mixed sources and/or low levels of target DNA (Taberlet et al. 1996;Morin et al. 2001). A common problem is the ability to obtain enough high-quality DNA for reliable genotyping, as opposed to tissue or blood samples that have significantly more target DNA and fewer inhibitors (Piggott and Taylor 2003a). A technique that is sometimes used to maximise the quantity of DNA available for PCR is performing a second elution phase at the end of the DNA extraction process, which allows for the elution of any retained DNA in the silica membrane of a spin column without diluting the first eluate (QIAGEN 2006). Despite having reduced DNA quantities remaining within the second eluate, it is considered that the amount of potential inhibitors remaining for a second elution is also reduced, therefore allowing for cleaner and better-quality DNA. With inhibition being a potential cause of genotyping failure (Ramón-Laca et al. 2015) using such a technique may improve the amplification rate for DNA extracted from bilby scats and may reduce the genotyping errors observed.

In order to establish whether DNA from faecal pellets can be used for reliable monitoring of bilbies, an understanding of the degradation of the DNA is required. The aims of this study were to examine the relationship between DNA degradation from bilby faecal pellets over time, and to determine whether the twostep elution protocol improves the amplification rate of DNA extracted from bilby faecal pellets. We expected that the rate of amplification of DNA would decline over time and the rate of genotyping errors, both false alleles and allelic dropouts, would increase over time as the DNA degrades. We also predicted that DNA amplified using a second eluate would increase the rate of amplification and decrease the rate of genotyping errors by providing higher-quality DNA through a reduction in potential inhibitors.

div.head: Faecal pellet collection and experimental design
div.p: Faecal pellets were collected from three captive male bilbies housed individually at Kanyana Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre in Lesmurdie, Western Australia. Over a 20-day period in January and February 2015, 63 samples were collected within 24 h of deposition. Captive individuals were used in this study in order to obtain an accurate deposition time, and to eliminate the possibility of additional environmental factors and varying diet amongst individuals to influence the rate of DNA degradation, all of which would be impossible to control for if faecal pellets were collected from a wild population.

Each pellet was placed on dry, prewashed sand in a 5 cm Â 5 cm square labelled ceramic dish and transported to the Department of Parks and Wildlife, Wildlife Research Centre at Woodvale, Western Australia. Samples were placed in a position allocated at random in an enclosure measuring 90 cm (W) Â 90 cm (L) Â 45 cm (H), constructed from 3-mm wire. The enclosure was covered by a sheet of 0.5-cm clear Perspex and secured onto a wooden pallet which was 15 cm off the ground. The enclosure was placed in the field on a concrete slab in a semishaded area with surrounding trees. The enclosure was used to prevent animals (e.g. foxes, crows) disturbing the pellets. The enclosure was kept on the pallet off the ground to prevent flooding of the dishes in case of rain. The Perspex prevented rain directly falling on the experiment whilst allowing normal air flow and sunlight. It allowed us to control potential rainfall impacting the scats and prematurely terminating the experiment and kept the effects of rainfall constant across the experimental period.

On each sampling day at Kanyana, three faecal pellets from each of the three individuals were collected and all samples were assigned to a single treatment period. Collection of faecal samples continued until a total of 21 pellets per individual were collected. The seven treatments covered the time periods in days (1, 7, 14, 21, 30, 90 and 180) of the duration between initial pellet collection from Kanyana and the harvesting of the pellets from Woodvale and immediate DNA extraction. The experiment was performed primarily over the summer months in order to best simulate the northern Western Australian conditions experienced within bilby habitat. The temperature conditions recorded in the Perth metropolitan area over the treatment period ranged from 0.8 C to 40.0 C with a relative humidity from 21% up to 99% (Bureau of Meteorology 2015).

div.head: DNA extraction
div.p: Extractions were undertaken using the QIAGEN QIAamp Fast DNA Stool MiniKit with modifications that included a wash of the faecal pellets (Piggott and Taylor 2003a), the use of Poly-A carrier RNA and an extended incubation period for DNA elution (Morin et al. 2001). The wash of epithelial cells from each pellet was performed with 1.5 mL to 5 mL of SLP buffer (see Deuter et al. 1995 for SLP buffer) followed by a 10-min incubation at 70 C (Piggott and Taylor 2003a). Carrier RNA was included in the process (Roeder et al. 2004) after the second incubation step to assist in the retention of the small quantities of target DNA within the membrane of the spin column, therefore enhancing the recovery of the DNA (Shaw et al. 2009;QIAGEN 2014). A two-step elution process was undertaken at the end of the extraction protocol. Elutions were performed using 50 mL of buffer ATE left to incubate at room temperature for 20 min and then spun in the centrifuge for 2 min in order to elute the DNA from the spin column. DNA was then pipetted into a labelled 1.5-mL microcentrifuge tube and the spin column placed back into the same collection tube for the second elution step. A second 50 mL of buffer ATE was then added to the spin column and left to incubate for a further 20 min before eluting the DNA, which was then pipetted into another labelled 1.5-mL microcentrifuge tube. DNA samples were stored in a À20 C freezer until PCR.

div.head: PCR amplification and fragment analysis
div.p: PCR amplification was undertaken using three bilby-specific polymorphic microsatellite markers (Moritz et al. 1997;Smith et al. 2009) (refer to Table 1) amplified in a single multiplex. Three PCR replicates using the Qiagen Multiplex PCR Plus Kit were used for each scat sample. PCRs were carried out using the same Eppendorf Thermal Cycler for every PCR. For each PCR replicate, 2 mL of DNA was used in a 12.5-mL reaction with PCR cycling and annealing conditions as per the protocol recommended by the manufacturer for the multiplex kit. A modified extension period of 30 s per cycle was used (Smith and Hughes 2008), rather than the manufacturer's recommendation of 90 s.

Plates containing PCR products were stored in a À20 C freezer until being prepared for fragment analysis. PCR product was analysed on an ABI3730XL Sequencer and sized using Genescan LIZ 500 size standard (Applied Biosystems).

Scoring of alleles was undertaken using GeneMapper Software 5.0. Results were reviewed manually in order to ensure correct scoring of alleles and to confirm genotyping errors, both the presence of false alleles and allelic dropouts. The Day 1 treatment period samples were used as references to establish genotyping errors, as these produced identical results across all faecal pellets and PCR replicates for each individual. Allelic dropouts were recorded as per the definition and protocol employed by Broquet and Petit (2004), where one allele from an individual that exhibited heterozygosity at a locus in the reference genotype was not observed in the replicate sample (either extraction or PCR) for that individual. An allele was considered a false allele where DNA amplification was successful but an allele was observed that was inconsistent with the reference genotypes (Bonin et al. 2004;Broquet and Petit 2004;Waits and Paetkau 2005).

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: Repeated-measures mixed-model ANOVA was used to compare the effects of elution and time on the amplification, false allele and allelic dropout rates. The first repeated-measures factor, elution, consisted of two levels, Elution 1 and 2. The second repeated-measures factor was time, and consisted of seven periods when scats were harvested: 1, 7, 14, 21, 30, 90 and 180 days. Individual animals were included in the model as a random, blocking factor, though we neither report the statistics of this factor nor the interaction of this factor with elution or CTA CAA GTC TGA TAA TTC CAG GC Moritz et al. (1997) time. The Greenhouse-Geisser Epsilon (GG-P) was used because it is a more conservative adjustment of the F ratio. All proportions were arcsine-transformed (Zar 1999) into degrees before analyses.

div.head: Results
div.p: DNA amplification was successful across all three loci (B22, B41 and B55), providing consistent results for all three individuals for the first two treatment periods (Days 1 and 7) across Elution 1 (Appendix 1). Although these genotypes were obtained from faecal DNA rather than tissue or blood, the fact that genotypes were 100% consistent across all extraction and PCR replicates for these first two treatments indicates that these results could be reliably used as genotyping references for which subsequent results could be adequately compared to assess amplification success and determine genotyping errors. Time had a significant effect on the amplification rates of bilby faecal DNA (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P < 0.001). As time progressed for both Elutions 1 and 2, the ability to amplify DNA from bilby scats decreased, although at no point did it achieve consistent non-amplification over the 180 days of this experiment (Fig. 1). There was also a significant difference in the rate of amplification between the two elution steps (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P < 0.001). A higher proportion of samples were successfully genotyped from Elution 1 than from Elution 2 (Fig. 1). The interaction between time and elution was also significant (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P = 0.002). The amplification rate of DNA from the second eluate decreased with time at a higher rate from the 14-day treatment period than the DNA from the first eluate (Fig. 1a). There were no significant main effects or interaction of time and elution on the proportion of false alleles recorded within individual genotypes (Table 2).

Time had a significant effect on the rate of allelic dropout (Table 2: P < 0.001; GG-P = 0.015), with the proportion of allelic dropouts increasing over time (Fig. 1). There was a significant effect of elution on allelic dropout (Table 2: P = 0.006; GG-P = 0.006). There were more allelic dropouts observed from DNA in the second eluate than using DNA from a single elution step (Fig. 1). There was no significant interaction of time and elution on allelic dropout (Table 2).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This study set out to determine how age since deposition affects the amplification of DNA from bilby scats. Our study showed that amplification rate decreases and allelic dropout rate increases in DNA extracted from bilby scats as time since deposition increases. We also found that a two-step elution process, contrary to our initial hypothesis, does not increase amplification rates or decrease error rates in DNA extracted from bilby scats.

Despite the decrease in amplification rate over time, even at 90 and 180 days since deposition, we were able to successfully amplify DNA from faecal pellets and clearly identify the three individuals used in this study, with the rate only dropping as low as 63% for Elution 1 (at 90 days) and 21% for Elution 2 (at 180 days) (Fig. 1a). Our results show that there is potential to identify bilby individuals that were in a particular area up to the six-month time frame. For extracting DNA from bilby scats, from both a time and cost-effectiveness perspective, the optimal timeframe for scat collection would be within two weeks from deposition, with ~99% amplification success for one elution step being achieved and low rates (<5%) of genotyping error (Fig. 1). As with other faecal DNA and microsatellite studies (Lucchini et al. 2002;Piggott 2004;Miller et al. 2010), allelic dropout was the most common genotyping error associated with this experiment. This is consistent with previous findings by Morin et al. (2001) whereby allelic dropouts are more prevalent when the original quantity of template DNA is low, which appears to be the case in relation to our amplification rate results: as amplification rates decrease, due to the reduction in DNA quantity and quality over time, the rate of allelic dropout increases.

The low rate of false alleles observed in this study is likely to be a result of the low presence of false alleles across the experiment generally, with non-amplification being more likely than the production of false alleles. Where false alleles were observed these were generally sporadic (Morin et al. 2001), only present in single samples and not often reproduced across scat samples from the same individual or PCRs.

The premise that a two-step elution process would produce higher-quality DNA due to fewer inhibitors in the second elution phase was not upheld in this study. The ability to amplify DNA from Elution 2 samples showed that DNA was still in the spin column after the first elution, particularly for the first two time treatments, however Elution 1 samples provided greater than 60% amplification throughout the experimental period (Fig. 1a) and exhibited a lower allelic dropout rate than the second eluate (Fig. 1b). The amplification rates of the second round of eluted DNA decreased at a much quicker rate from the 14-day treatment period compared with the first eluate (Fig. 1a). It is also reasonable to expect that this may be the case because a reduction in available epithelial cells from which to obtain DNA from the samples over time could also mean that there will inevitably be less DNA for the second elution phase, too low to result in successful DNA amplification and subsequent genotyping. The consequence of using Elution 2 to determine genotypes is that the rate of amplification decreased significantly quicker than that for Elution 1 over the same period, therefore should pellets be collected that are more than a week old the likelihood of non-amplification and the risk of genotyping errors being observed will increase. Based on these results it is not considered worthwhile performing a twostep elution method as part of the DNA extraction protocol for bilby scats and it would be more cost-effective and efficient to complete more PCR replicates using just one elution. Additional methods that may also improve the success and efficiency of DNA extraction and PCR processes, that were not tested as part of this experiment, include combining eluates to increase the amount of total DNA in the final sample and utilising quantitative PCR to better understand the quantity of DNA before further fragment analyses.

Several factors such as rainfall and the diet of individuals are likely to impact DNA preservation on faecal pellets or may result in different inhibition in the amplification of bilby DNA. Rainfall has been identified as being a prominent factor in the decay rates of scat DNA (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b). In our study we controlled for the effects of rainfall by using a clear Perspex roof over our experimental treatments. This ensured that the effects of rainfall events were constant across the time treatments and prevented a catastrophic rain event prematurely terminating the experiment but allowed natural sunlight and UV penetration. In the field, the rate of DNA decay may well increase after rainfall events and result in more rapid overall decay, with spikes in decay rate rather than the more evenly decreasing relationship observed in this study. Therefore, the occurrence of rain should be considered before sampling bilby scats in the field for DNA extraction.

The diet of the captive bilbies used in this study consisted of mealworms, seed, dog biscuits, fruit and vegetables. The diet of wild bilbies includes lepidopteran larvae, termites, ants, grasshoppers, spiders and beetles, seed, bulbs (Cyperus bulbosus) and fungi (Burbidge et al. 1988;Gibson 2001;Southgate and Carthew 2006). Differences in diet may lead to differences in decay rates of faecal DNA, particularly if the diet affects the moisture content within the pellets. DNA from faecal pellets containing more moisture may decay at a higher rate, similar to that due to increased moisture caused by rainfall (Piggott 2004;Brinkman et al. 2010b). Since the captive animals used in this study were all fed the same diet, this variation was controlled for in our design. Overall, however, since water conservation is a priority for bilbies, and as such very little water is lost through excretion of faeces and urine (Gibson and Hume 2000a, 2000b, 2004;Gibson et al. 2002), the inherent dryness of bilby faecal pellets likely contributes to the long viability of the faecal DNA.

The environment in which bilby faecal pellets are deposited may also influence the ability to obtain viable DNA from them. Bilby faecal pellets can be found either in the open but more often than not around foraging sites as well as buried within the spoil of diggings or burrows. The faecal pellets collected from the captive individuals in this experiment were found in both situations, either on top of the sand in the enclosure or buried within it whilst the individual had been foraging. It is possible that the act of burying the scats could have an effect on the number of epithelial cells retained on the scats to be able to be washed off for DNA extraction. In contrast, faecal pellets from wild populations that are located in the open are exposed to wind and direct UV radiation, which buried pellets are not, and the DNA may therefore degrade more rapidly as a result of this.

In addition to the factors mentioned above, for wild bilby populations, seasonal changes both in diet, as a result of resource availability (Gibson 2001), and the external environmental conditions (Piggott 2004) such as humidity, rainfall, temperature, UV radiation and ash content if collected from recently burnt habitat, may also influence the ability to extract bilby DNA and successfully genotype individuals. The order in which the selected faecal pellet was deposited may also influence the amount of DNA on the pellet (Walker et al. 2009), highlighting the need for multiple or repeat extractions where an initial extraction may not have been successful.

Incorporating genetics as a component of an overall conservation and management strategy for bilbies not only allows for the identification of individuals and the potential for monitoring populations, it may also assist in gaining a better understanding of the movement of individuals across the landscape and survivorship over time (if an individual is identified through faecal DNA at different locations or on multiple monitoring trips). It could also be used in further population genetics studies (Southgate and Adams 1994;Moritz et al. 1997), including assessment of population fragmentation across the Pilbara and Kimberley regions of Western Australia and across Australia as a whole.

This study found that, under seminatural conditions, viable DNA exists on bilby faecal pellets for a long period and can be amplified with a 99% success rate and low error rates up to 14 days after deposition. The amplification rate decreases, and allelic dropout rates increase, gradually with time, but DNA can still be successfully amplified at rates above 80% and error rates below 11% at 30 days, and amplification rates above 60% and error rates below 15% at 90-180 days. We found that a second elution step was unnecessary. DNA was more successfully amplified using the first eluate with fewer allelic dropouts and a decreased rate of decline in amplification rates. This means that DNA can be successfully amplified from bilby faecal pellets for a long period after deposition, which can be useful for obtaining genetic samples for population monitoring programs and studies on population genetics.
